claim: SET-32 methylates histone H3 in vitro
source: We first tested SET-32's ability to methylate each of the four core histone proteins, and found that GST-SET-32 methylated free and nucleosomal H3, but not H2A, H2B, or H4 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by HMT assay data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating methylation of H3 but not other histones

claim: The Y448F mutation abolishes the HMT activity of SET-32 on H3
source: The Y448F mutation abolished the HMT activity of GST-SET-32 on H3 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1B showing loss of HMT activity with Y448F mutation

claim: SET-32 specifically methylates lysine 23 of histone H3
source: GST-SET-32 was able to methylate every mutant H3, except for H3K23L (Figure 1C), suggesting that the lysine 23 is SET-32's target.
evidence: Supported by HMT assay data with lysine mutants showing only K23L mutation prevents methylation

claim: SET-32 catalyzes mono-, di-, and tri-methylation at H3K23
source: We then performed mass spectrometry on GST-SET-32-treated H3, and detected mono, di, and tri-methylation at the K23 position (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis showing H3K23me1, me2, and me3

claim: Untreated control H3 has no H3K23 methylation
source: The untreated control H3 had no H3K23 methylation.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data comparing treated and untreated H3

claim: SET-32 does not methylate other lysine residues of H3 besides K23
source: We did not detect methylation at any of the other lysine residues of H3.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis showing no methylation at other lysines

claim: oma-1 dsRNA feeding triggers a dramatic increase in H3K23me3 in wild type animals
source: In WT animals, oma-1 dsRNA feeding triggered no detectable change in H3K23me1, a modest increase in H3K23me2, and a dramatic increase in H3K23me3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The peak of H3K23me3 corresponds to the trigger region of the oma-1 dsRNA and spreads approximately 0.5 kb upstream and 1 kb downstream of the oma-1 gene boundaries
source: The peak of H3K23me3 corresponds to the trigger region of the oma-1 dsRNA, and spreads approximately 0.5 kb upstream and 1 kb downstream of the oma-1 gene boundaries.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq coverage analysis at the oma-1 locus

claim: GFP dsRNA and no dsRNA controls do not show any H3K23 methylation at oma-1
source: The GFP dsRNA and no dsRNA controls did not show any H3K23 methylation at oma-1.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data comparing different dsRNA treatments

claim: H3K23me3 and H3K9me3 show closely overlapping profiles at the oma-1 locus after dsRNA feeding
source: In order to compare H3K23me3 with a previously described dsRNA-induced histone mark, we performed side-by-side analysis of H3K23me3 and H3K9me3 and observed closely overlapping profiles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by comparative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: H3K23me3 can be induced at smg-1 by dsRNA feeding
source: To verify that H3K23me3 can be induced at other genes, we fed worms with smg-1 dsRNA and confirmed that H3K23me3 was enriched at the target chromatin in response to smg-1 dsRNA, with a profile similar to H3K9me3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data at the smg-1 locus shown in Figure 2B

claim: H3K23me3 at oma-1 persists for four generations after RNA-feeding has been stopped
source: Similar to H3K9me3, H3K23me3 at oma-1 persisted for four generations after the RNA-feeding had been stopped (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by heritable RNAi experiment data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: RNAi-mediated H3K23me3 is a transgenerational epigenetic effect in C. elegans
source: These results indicate that RNAi-mediated H3K23me3 is a transgenerational epigenetic effect in C. elegans.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of H3K23me3 across multiple generations after dsRNA removal

claim: The genomic distribution of H3K23me3 is highly similar to the genomic distribution of H3K9me3
source: The genomic distribution of H3K23me3 was highly similar to the genomic distribution of H3K9me3 (Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 3A-B and supplements

claim: H3K23me3 is enriched at constitutive heterochromatin domains including the left and right arms of the five autosomes and the left tip of the X chromosome
source: We observed H3K23me3 enrichment at constitutive heterochromatin domains: the left and right arms of the five autosomes and the left tip of the X chromosome.
evidence: Supported by whole-genome ChIP-seq coverage analysis

claim: The highest peaks of H3K23me3 are observed at the meiotic pairing centers
source: Like H3K9me3, we observed the highest peaks of H3K23me3 at the meiotic paring centers (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq coverage plots showing peaks at pairing centers

claim: H3K23me2 and H3K23me1 have a relatively uniform distribution in the genome
source: H3K23me2 and H3K23me1 seem to have a relative uniform distribution in the genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome ChIP-seq coverage analysis

claim: H3K9me3 shows statistically significant enrichment at the arms compared to the middle of each chromosome
source: As expected, H3K9me3 shows statistically significant enrichment at the arms compared to the middle of each chromosome.
evidence: Supported by boxplot analysis of ChIP-seq data

claim: H3K23me3 displays enrichment at the chromosome arms, however, to a lesser extent than H3K9me3
source: H3K23me3 also displays enrichment at the arms, however, to a lesser extent.
evidence: Supported by boxplot analysis comparing arms and middle regions

claim: H3K23me3 and H3K9me3 show high correlation across the genome with a Pearson coefficient of 0.8
source: In order to further assess the correspondence of H3K23me3 and H3K9me3, we plotted whole genome coverage of both modifications on a scatter plot and observed a high correlation (Pearson coefficient = 0.8) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by scatter plot analysis of whole-genome ChIP-seq data

claim: H3K23me3 is enriched at endogenous targets of nuclear RNAi
source: These data demonstrate that H3K23me3 is enriched at endogenous nuclear RNAi targets.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data at multiple endogenous target loci

claim: At endogenous targets, H3K23me3 closely resembles the H3K9me3 signal
source: At the endogenous targets, H3K23me3 closely resembles the H3K9me3 signal (Figure 3C,E–G).
evidence: Supported by comparative ChIP-seq coverage plots at endogenous targets

claim: The actively transcribed cdc-42 locus does not show enrichment of either H3K9me3 or H3K23me3
source: By contrast, the actively transcribed cdc-42 locus did not show any enrichment of either H3K9me3 or H3K23me3 (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data at the cdc-42 locus

claim: Nuclear RNAi-induced H3K23me3 is greatly enriched in the germline
source: By comparing the glp-1 mutant and WT worms, we were able to determine that nuclear RNAi-induced H3K23me3 is indeed greatly enriched in the germline (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of ChIP-seq data between glp-1 mutant and WT

claim: H3K23me3 is present in both soma and germline
source: However, H3K23me3 was still present in the glp-1 mutant animals at both nuclear RNAi targets and globally, indicating that H3K23me3 occurs in both soma and germline.
evidence: Supported by detection of H3K23me3 in glp-1 mutants which lack germline

claim: hrde-1 mutant worms show greatly reduced H3K23me3 at the oma-1 locus after dsRNA feeding compared to WT
source: As expected, hrde-1 and set-32 mutant worms showed greatly reduced H3K23me3 at the oma-1 locus compared to WT.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data comparing mutants to WT at oma-1

claim: set-32 mutant worms show greatly reduced H3K23me3 at the oma-1 locus after dsRNA feeding compared to WT
source: As expected, hrde-1 and set-32 mutant worms showed greatly reduced H3K23me3 at the oma-1 locus compared to WT.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data comparing mutants to WT at oma-1

claim: met-2 set-25 double mutant and WT animals induce similar, high levels of H3K23me3 at oma-1 after dsRNA feeding
source: By contrast, oma-1 RNAi in the double HMT mutant, met-2 set-25, and the WT animals induced similar, high levels of H3K23me3, indicating that SET-32 has a specific role in H3K23 methylation not shared by the other two HMTs (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data comparing met-2 set-25 mutant to WT

claim: SET-32 has a specific role in H3K23 methylation not shared by MET-2 and SET-25
source: By contrast, oma-1 RNAi in the double HMT mutant, met-2 set-25, and the WT animals induced similar, high levels of H3K23me3, indicating that SET-32 has a specific role in H3K23 methylation not shared by the other two HMTs (Figure 4A).
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirement of SET-32 vs MET-2/SET-25 for H3K23me3

claim: The regulation of H3K23me3 at nuclear RNAi targets is complex and likely involves other HMTs
source: These findings indicate that the regulation of H3K23me3 at nuclear RNAi targets is complex, and likely to involve other HMTs.
evidence: Inferred from variable genetic requirements at different endogenous targets

claim: There is a strong loss of H3K23me3 at endogenous nuclear RNAi targets in hrde-1 mutant animals
source: However, we did see a strong loss of H3K23me3 at endogenous nuclear RNAi targets in both the hrde-1 and set-32 mutant animals and weaker H3K23me3 reduction in the met-2 set-25 double mutant animals (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome analysis of ChIP-seq data at endogenous targets

claim: There is a strong loss of H3K23me3 at endogenous nuclear RNAi targets in set-32 mutant animals
source: However, we did see a strong loss of H3K23me3 at endogenous nuclear RNAi targets in both the hrde-1 and set-32 mutant animals and weaker H3K23me3 reduction in the met-2 set-25 double mutant animals (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome analysis of ChIP-seq data at endogenous targets

claim: There is a weaker H3K23me3 reduction at endogenous nuclear RNAi targets in met-2 set-25 double mutant animals
source: However, we did see a strong loss of H3K23me3 at endogenous nuclear RNAi targets in both the hrde-1 and set-32 mutant animals and weaker H3K23me3 reduction in the met-2 set-25 double mutant animals (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome analysis of ChIP-seq data at endogenous targets

claim: The majority of SET-32-dependent genes overlap with HRDE-1-dependent genes
source: We then performed a Venn diagram analysis and found that the majority of SET-32-dependent genes overlapped with HRDE-1-dependent genes (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis of gene lists

claim: There are over 150 SET-32-dependent H3K23me3 genes
source: There are over 150 SET-32-dependent H3K23me3 genes, in contrast there are only 40 MET-2 SET-25-dependent H3K23me3 genes.
evidence: Supported by gene counting from ChIP-seq analysis

claim: There are only 40 MET-2 SET-25-dependent H3K23me3 genes
source: There are over 150 SET-32-dependent H3K23me3 genes, in contrast there are only 40 MET-2 SET-25-dependent H3K23me3 genes.
evidence: Supported by gene counting from ChIP-seq analysis

claim: There are three times as many MET-2 SET-25-dependent H3K9me3 genes as there are SET-32-dependent H3K9me3 genes
source: In comparison, there are three times as many MET-2 SET-25-dependent H3K9me3 genes as there are SET-32-dependent H3K9me3 genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis of H3K9me3-dependent genes

claim: 61.4% of hrde-1-dependent H3K23me3 genes are enriched for repeat DNA of varying classes
source: In this analysis, we found that while no class of genes was enriched in these targets, 61.4% of the genes were enriched for repeat DNA of varying classes (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by repeat analysis of hrde-1-dependent genes

claim: The majority of repeats in hrde-1-dependent H3K23me3 genes are low complexity and DNA repeats
source: The majority of repeats were low complexity and DNA repeats (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by repeat class analysis

claim: 4.37% of hrde-1-dependent H3K23me3 genes containing repeats contain LTRs
source: However, there was also an enrichment of LTRs (4.37% percent of genes containing repeats contained LTRs) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by repeat class analysis

claim: Nuclear RNAi is an evolutionarily conserved pathway in which small RNAs mediate transcriptional silencing and heterochromatin formation
source: Nuclear RNAi is an evolutionarily conserved pathway in which small RNAs mediate transcriptional silencing and heterochromatin formation (Wassenegger, 2000; Sienski et al., 2012; Pezic et al., 2014; Rechavi et al., 2014; Martienssen and Moazed, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Nuclear RNAi plays an important role in genome stability and germline development
source: Nuclear RNAi plays an important role in genome stability and germline development.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: In the C. elegans germline, nuclear RNAi relies on the Argonaute protein HRDE-1
source: In the C. elegans germline, nuclear RNAi relies on the Argonaute protein HRDE-1 (Ashe et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2012; Shirayama et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: HRDE-1 binds secondary siRNAs and recruits nuclear RNAi factors to genomic sites of RNAi
source: In current models, HRDE-1 binds secondary siRNAs and recruits nuclear RNAi factors, including chromatin modifying enzymes and remodeling factors, to genomic sites of RNAi.
evidence: Based on current models in the field

claim: Over 150 genomic loci in C. elegans are de-silenced and/or lose repressive chromatin modifications in nuclear RNAi-deficient mutants
source: We and others have characterized over 150 genomic loci in C. elegans that are de-silenced and/or lose repressive chromatin modifications in nuclear RNAi-deficient mutants, the so-called 'endogenous targets' (Ni et al., 2014; McMurchy et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by the authors and others

claim: Nuclear RNAi-mediated silencing can be experimentally triggered at actively transcribed genes by exogenous dsRNA administration or piRNA
source: In addition, nuclear RNAi-mediated silencing can be experimentally triggered at actively transcribed genes by exogenous dsRNA administration or piRNA ('exogenous targets') (Ahringer, 2006; Vastenhouw et al., 2006; Guang et al., 2010; Ashe et al., 2012; Gu et al., 2012; Shirayama et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: Silencing at exogenous targets can persist for multiple generations
source: Silencing at the exogenous targets can persist for multiple generations.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: Germline nuclear RNAi-deficient mutants in C. elegans exhibit progressive sterility under heat stress (Mrt phenotype)
source: Germline nuclear RNAi-deficient mutants in C. elegans exhibit several phenotypes, including progressive sterility under heat stress (Mrt phenotype) and large-scale de-silencing and chromatin decompaction at the endogenous targets (Guang et al., 2010; Ashe et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2012; Shirayama et al., 2012; Weiser et al., 2017; Fields and Kennedy, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Germline nuclear RNAi-deficient mutants in C. elegans exhibit large-scale de-silencing and chromatin decompaction at the endogenous targets
source: Germline nuclear RNAi-deficient mutants in C. elegans exhibit several phenotypes, including progressive sterility under heat stress (Mrt phenotype) and large-scale de-silencing and chromatin decompaction at the endogenous targets (Guang et al., 2010; Ashe et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2012; Shirayama et al., 2012; Weiser et al., 2017; Fields and Kennedy, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 are known nuclear RNAi-induced histone modifications in C. elegans
source: There are two known nuclear RNAi-induced histone modifications in C. elegans: trimethylation at lysine 27 and lysine 9 of histone H3 (H3K27me3 and H3K9me3).
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: H3K9me3 is the best studied nuclear RNAi-induced histone modification
source: The best studied nuclear RNAi-induced histone modification is H3K9me3, however the function of this histone modification in nuclear RNAi remains unknown (Burton et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2012; Mao et al., 2015; Kalinava et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: H3K9me3 is not essential for silencing maintenance if HRDE-1 is present
source: Prior models assumed that the heterochromatin mark was required for transcriptional silencing in nuclear RNAi, but surprisingly, H3K9me3 is not essential for silencing maintenance if HRDE-1 is present (Kalinava et al., 2017; McMurchy et al., 2017; Woodhouse et al., 2018; Lev et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: MET-2 and SET-25 function sequentially for H3K9 methylation
source: Two HMTs, MET-2 and SET-25, are suggested to function sequentially for H3K9 methylation (Towbin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: In embryos, MET-2 and SET-25 appear to be the sole contributors of H3K9 methylation
source: In embryos, MET-2 and SET-25 appear to be the sole contributors of H3K9 methylation (Towbin et al., 2012; Garrigues et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: In adults, nuclear RNAi-mediated H3K9me3 is dependent on SET-32 in addition to MET-2 and SET-25
source: However, in adults, nuclear RNAi-mediated H3K9me3 is dependent on a third additional HMT, SET-32 (Mao et al., 2015; Kalinava et al., 2017; Spracklin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: MET-2, SET-25 and SET-32 are not functionally equivalent
source: While MET-2, SET-25 and SET-32 are all required for the formation of H3K9me3, they are not functionally equivalent.
evidence: Inferred from differential requirements in different contexts

claim: MET-2, but not SET-25, is required for DNA replication stress survival
source: MET-2, but not SET-25, is required for DNA replication stress survival (Padeken et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: SET-25 and SET-32, but not MET-2, are required for the silencing of a piRNA-targeted reporter gene
source: SET-25 and SET-32, but not MET-2, are required for the silencing of a piRNA-targeted reporter gene (Ashe et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: SET-32 and, to a lesser extent, SET-25 are required for silencing establishment
source: In addition, while MET-2, SET-25, and SET-32 were all dispensable for silencing maintenance in nuclear RNAi, SET-32 and, to a lesser extent, SET-25 are required for silencing establishment (Kalinava et al., 2018; Woodhouse et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: MET-2, SET-25, and SET-32 are dispensable for silencing maintenance in nuclear RNAi
source: In addition, while MET-2, SET-25, and SET-32 were all dispensable for silencing maintenance in nuclear RNAi, SET-32 and, to a lesser extent, SET-25 are required for silencing establishment (Kalinava et al., 2018; Woodhouse et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: From the embryonic stage to adulthood, the two most prominently methylated lysines of histone H3 in C. elegans are H3K27 and H3K23
source: From the embryonic stage to adulthood, the two most prominently methylated lysines of histone H3 are H3K27 and H3K23, while H3K9me is proportionally much lower (Vandamme et al., 2015; Sidoli et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: H3K9me is proportionally much lower than H3K27me and H3K23me in C. elegans from embryonic stage to adulthood
source: From the embryonic stage to adulthood, the two most prominently methylated lysines of histone H3 are H3K27 and H3K23, while H3K9me is proportionally much lower (Vandamme et al., 2015; Sidoli et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: H3K23me has been suggested as a heterochromatin mark in C. elegans
source: H3K23me has been suggested as a heterochromatin mark in C. elegans (Vandamme et al., 2015; Sidoli et al., 2016b) and Tetrahymena (Papazyan et al., 2014) and is involved in DNA damage control (Papazyan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: H3K23me has been suggested as a heterochromatin mark in Tetrahymena
source: H3K23me has been suggested as a heterochromatin mark in C. elegans (Vandamme et al., 2015; Sidoli et al., 2016b) and Tetrahymena (Papazyan et al., 2014) and is involved in DNA damage control (Papazyan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: H3K23me is involved in DNA damage control
source: H3K23me has been suggested as a heterochromatin mark in C. elegans (Vandamme et al., 2015; Sidoli et al., 2016b) and Tetrahymena (Papazyan et al., 2014) and is involved in DNA damage control (Papazyan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Almost all histone lysine methylation is catalyzed by SET-domain containing histone methyltransferases
source: Almost all histone lysine methylation is catalyzed by SET-domain containing histone methyltransferases (Cheng et al., 2005; Qian and Zhou, 2006; Husmann and Gozani, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Different HMTs can target different lysine residues with high specificity despite sharing core catalytic motifs in the SET domain
source: Although different HMTs share core catalytic motifs in the SET domain, they can target different lysine residues with high specificity (Cheng et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: In Tetrahymena, the SET-domain containing enzyme EZL3 is required for H3K23me3 in vivo
source: In Tetrahymena, the SET-domain containing enzyme, EZL3, is required for H3K23me3 in vivo (Papazyan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Loss of SET-32 causes reduced levels of H3K23me1 and H3K23me2 in C. elegans
source: In C. elegans, loss of SET-32 causes reduced levels of H3K23me1 and H3K23me2 (H3K23me3 was not tested) (Woodhouse et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: No H3K23 HMT has been biochemically validated at the time of this manuscript publication
source: No H3K23 HMT has been biochemically validated at the time of this manuscript publication.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field at time of publication

claim: H3K23me3 at nuclear RNAi targets is dependent on HRDE-1 and SET-32
source: In addition, H3K23me3 at nuclear RNAi targets is dependent on HRDE-1 and SET-32, and, to a lesser extent, MET-2 and SET-25.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data in mutant strains

claim: H3K23me3 at nuclear RNAi targets is dependent on MET-2 and SET-25 to a lesser extent than HRDE-1 and SET-32
source: In addition, H3K23me3 at nuclear RNAi targets is dependent on HRDE-1 and SET-32, and, to a lesser extent, MET-2 and SET-25.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data in mutant strains

claim: SET-32 contains four conserved catalytic motifs in the SET-domain
source: There are four conserved catalytic motifs in the SET-domain family proteins, all of which are found in SET-32 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Cheng et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and citation

claim: The tyrosine residue at position 448 in motif IV is predicted to be one of the catalytic residues of SET-32
source: The highly conserved tyrosine residue at position 448 in motif IV is predicted to be one of the catalytic residues of SET-32.
evidence: Based on sequence conservation and structural predictions

claim: C. elegans provides a number of unique advantages for the study of nuclear RNAi
source: C. elegans provides a number of unique advantages for the study of nuclear RNAi (Weiser and Kim, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published review

claim: Genetic screens have identified numerous protein factors involved in the nuclear RNAi pathway
source: Genetic screens have identified numerous protein factors involved in this pathway.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: H3K23me3 is a constitutive heterochromatin mark
source: Our results are consistent with previous reports that H3K23me3 is a constitutive heterochromatin mark (Papazyan et al., 2014; Vandamme et al., 2015; Sidoli et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by data in this study and citations to previous reports

claim: H3K23me3 correlates highly with H3K9me3
source: Our data confirm previous reports that H3K23me3 is heterochromatic in distribution and correlates highly with H3K9me3.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq data

claim: H3K23 methylation was discovered in alfalfa in 1990
source: H3K23 methylation was discovered in alfalfa in 1990 (Waterborg, 1990) and has subsequently been found in yeast, Tetrahymena, C. elegans, mouse, rat, pig and human (Waterborg, 1990; Garcia et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013; Papazyan et al., 2014; Vandamme et al., 2015; Sidoli et al., 2016b; Su et al., 2016; Fišerová et al., 2017; Myers et al., 2018; Woodhouse et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to original discovery

claim: H3K23 methylation has been found in yeast, Tetrahymena, C. elegans, mouse, rat, pig and human
source: H3K23 methylation was discovered in alfalfa in 1990 (Waterborg, 1990) and has subsequently been found in yeast, Tetrahymena, C. elegans, mouse, rat, pig and human (Waterborg, 1990; Garcia et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013; Papazyan et al., 2014; Vandamme et al., 2015; Sidoli et al., 2016b; Su et al., 2016; Fišerová et al., 2017; Myers et al., 2018; Woodhouse et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies

claim: H3K23 is the second most highly methylated lysine of H3 in C. elegans
source: H3K23 is the second most highly methylated lysine of H3 in C. elegans (Papazyan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: This study discovered the first biochemically validated H3K23 histone methyltransferase
source: In addition, this study discovered the first biochemically validated H3K23 histone methyltransferase (HMT) and demonstrated that H3K23me3 can be experimentally induced at RNAi target genes.
evidence: Supported by the in vitro HMT assay data presented in the study

claim: H3K23me3 can be experimentally induced at RNAi target genes
source: In addition, this study discovered the first biochemically validated H3K23 histone methyltransferase (HMT) and demonstrated that H3K23me3 can be experimentally induced at RNAi target genes.
evidence: Supported by dsRNA feeding experiments and ChIP-seq data

claim: Nuclear RNAi induces multiple heterochromatin marks including H3K9me3, H3K27me3, and H3K23me3
source: Previous studies identified H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 as nuclear RNAi-mediated histone modifications (Gu et al., 2012; Mao et al., 2015). This study adds H3K23me3 to the list.
evidence: Supported by data in this study and citations to previous studies

claim: Different marks at nuclear RNAi targets are deposited by different HMTs: MET-2 and SET-25 for H3K9me3, MES-2 for H3K27me3, and SET-32 and unknown other HMT(s) for H3K23me3
source: Based on these results, we propose that the revised model should include the following features. (1) Different marks at nuclear RNAi targets are deposited by different HMTs: MET-2 and SET-25 for H3K9me3, MES-2 for H3K27me3, and SET-32 and unknown other HMT(s) for H3K23me3.
evidence: Inferred from genetic requirements and biochemical data

claim: The genetic requirement of SET-32 for H3K9me3 suggests that H3K23me3 promotes H3K9me3
source: (2) The genetic requirement of SET-32 for H3K9me3 suggests that H3K23me3 promotes H3K9me3.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SET-32 is required for both H3K23me3 and H3K9me3

claim: At some endogenous nuclear RNAi targets, H3K9me3 and H3K23me3 appear to be mutually dependent
source: (3) At some of the endogenous nuclear RNAi targets, H3K9me3 and H3K23me3 appear to be mutually dependent.
evidence: Inferred from variable genetic requirements at different loci

claim: H3K27me3 is largely independent of H3K9me3 and H3K23me3
source: (4) H3K27me3 is largely independent of H3K9me3 and H3K23me3 (Kalinava et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: SET-32 is dispensable for silencing maintenance when in the presence of wild-type HRDE-1
source: SET-32 is dispensable for silencing maintenance when in the presence of wild-type HRDE-1.
evidence: Based on published studies

claim: set-32 hrde-1 double mutants show enhanced de-silencing when compared to hrde-1 single mutants
source: However, set-32 hrde-1 double mutants show enhanced de-silencing when compared to hrde-1 single mutants (Kalinava et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: H3K23me3 may function as a failsafe or backup silencing mechanism in silencing maintenance
source: These results suggest a conditional requirement of H3K23me3 for silencing maintenance, possibly to function as a failsafe or backup silencing mechanism.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of genetic data

claim: SET-32 is required for silencing establishment at both exogenous dsRNA targets and endogenous targets
source: Recent studies have shown that SET-32 is required for silencing establishment at both exogenous dsRNA targets and endogenous targets (Kalinava et al., 2018; Woodhouse et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies
